claim: Persistent hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection is the leading cause of chronic liver cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) worldwide.
source: Persistent hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection is the leading cause of chronic liver cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) world wide (MacLachlan and Cowie, 2015; Di Bisceglie, 2009; An et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (MacLachlan and Cowie, 2015; Di Bisceglie, 2009; An et al., 2018).

claim: Chimpanzees remain the only animal model that supports the full HBV replication cycle.
source: Chimpanzees remain the only animal model that supports the full HBV replication cycle, while available hepatoma cell line models are unsuitable for delineating the molecular steps leading to tumorigenesis as they differ substantially from primary cells in their already tumor-derived gene expression profiles (Protzer, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Protzer, 2017).

claim: Available hepatoma cell line models are unsuitable for delineating the molecular steps leading to tumorigenesis as they differ substantially from primary cells in their already tumor-derived gene expression profiles.
source: Chimpanzees remain the only animal model that supports the full HBV replication cycle, while available hepatoma cell line models are unsuitable for delineating the molecular steps leading to tumorigenesis as they differ substantially from primary cells in their already tumor-derived gene expression profiles (Protzer, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Protzer, 2017).

claim: Primary hepatocytes present the gold standard model system for HBV research in vitro.
source: Primary hepatocytes present the gold standard model system for HBV research in vitro, with recent studies reporting on significant increases in the half-life of these cultures (Xiang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Xiang et al., 2019) and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Primary hepatocytes are difficult to obtain and cannot be expanded, limiting their availability for large-scale analyses.
source: However, primary cells are difficult to obtain and, since they cannot be expanded, are not usually available in quantities sufficient to perform large-scale analyses (Hu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Hu et al., 2019).

claim: Induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived hepatocytes are susceptible to HBV infection and support replication.
source: Induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived hepatocytes, which are susceptible to HBV infection and support replication, are also a useful model for studying host-virus determinants of replication (Kaneko et al., 2016; Nie et al., 2018; Sakurai et al., 2017; Xia et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Kaneko et al., 2016; Nie et al., 2018; Sakurai et al., 2017; Xia et al., 2017).

claim: iPSC-derived hepatocyte models cannot be patient derived, limiting the possibility of patient-specific personalized treatment approaches.
source: However, iPSC-derived hepatocyte models cannot be patient derived, confining studies to only ex vivo infection systems and limiting the possibility of patient-specific personalized treatment approaches (Torresi et al., 2019; Nantasanti et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Torresi et al., 2019; Nantasanti et al., 2016).

claim: Isolated adult hepatic cells can be expanded through multiple passages in optimized expansion medium without induction of genomic alterations.
source: In this culture system, isolated adult hepatic cells are expanded through multiple passages in an optimized expansion medium (EM) without induction of genomic alterations (Huch et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Huch et al., 2015).

claim: When switched to differentiation medium, liver organoid cultures differentiate into functional hepatocytes in vitro.
source: When switched to a differentiation medium (DM) where proliferation signals are removed and ductal (progenitor) fate is inhibited, liver organoid cultures differentiate into functional hepatocytes in vitro as exemplified by their polygonal cell shape (Figure 1A) and hepatocyte functions, including albumin production and cytochrome CYP3A4 expression and activity (Huch et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Huch et al., 2015) and by reference to Figure 1A showing morphological changes.

claim: Differentiated liver organoids produce albumin and express cytochrome CYP3A4.
source: When switched to a differentiation medium (DM) where proliferation signals are removed and ductal (progenitor) fate is inhibited, liver organoid cultures differentiate into functional hepatocytes in vitro as exemplified by their polygonal cell shape (Figure 1A) and hepatocyte functions, including albumin production and cytochrome CYP3A4 expression and activity (Huch et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Huch et al., 2015).

claim: HBV DNA was detected in organoid culture supernatants from 4 days post infection.
source: HBV DNA was detected in organoid culture supernatants from 4 days post infection, but not from the HI virus-infected cells, pointing to successful HBV replication (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Differentiated organoids maintained in DM were more efficiently infected and produced higher viral titers than organoids maintained in EM.
source: Differentiated organoids maintained in DM were more efficiently infected and produced higher viral titers than organoids maintained in EM (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1C-D.

claim: RNA intermediates necessary for protein production and viral replication (3.5 kb RNA transcript and total HBV RNA) were present in infected DM organoids.
source: The RNA intermediates necessary for protein production and viral replication (3.5 kb RNA transcript and total HBV RNA) were present in infected DM organoids and detected by nested polymerase chain reaction (PCR) analysis, but not in the HI virus-infected cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: HBV early antigen (HBeAg) was measured in supernatants of infected organoids.
source: As a further measure of active HBV replication, HBV early antigen (HBeAg) was also measured in supernatants of infected organoids and quantified (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Immunostaining using antibodies recognizing HBV core antigen (HBcAg) showed specific nuclear and cytoplasmic staining in multiple infected healthy donor liver organoid lines.
source: Immunostaining, using antibodies recognizing HBV core antigen (HBcAg), showed specific nuclear and cytoplasmic staining in multiple infected healthy donor liver organoid lines, confirming the presence of foci of HBV replication in HBV-infected cells predominantly in infected DM organoids (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: Infection of DM organoids resulted in the production of cccDNA.
source: Furthermore, infection of DM organoids resulted in the production of cccDNA, a definitive marker of HBV replication, as detected by a quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR)-based cccDNA detection method of intracellular HBV DNA after digestion with a nuclease to specifically remove non-cccDNA (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: cccDNA is a definitive marker of HBV replication.
source: Furthermore, infection of DM organoids resulted in the production of cccDNA, a definitive marker of HBV replication, as detected by a quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR)-based cccDNA detection method of intracellular HBV DNA after digestion with a nuclease to specifically remove non-cccDNA (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge in the field of HBV research.

claim: HBV replication, infection, and spread appeared to be persistent until 8 days after infection when viral production dropped significantly.
source: HBV replication, infection, and spread appeared to be persistent until 8 days after infection when viral production dropped significantly, likely because of the limited half-life of differentiated organoids in culture (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and includes speculation about the cause.

claim: Periodic culturing of the organoids in EM modestly extended the half-life of the infected cultures, where viral production was maintained for approximately 1 month post infection.
source: Periodic culturing of the organoids in EM in order to stimulate the recovery and proliferation of the organoids modestly extended the half-life of the infected cultures, where viral production was maintained for approximately 1 month post infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Donor-specific differences in efficiency of HBV infection were observed consistent with variable HBV permissiveness of primary human hepatocytes.
source: Donor-specific differences in efficiency of HBV infection were observed consistent with variable HBV permissiveness of primary human hepatocytes (Shlomai et al., 2014), while HBV infection was observed with similar efficiency in different passages of the same donor line (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–D and a citation to published literature (Shlomai et al., 2014).

claim: HBV infection was observed with similar efficiency in different passages of the same donor line.
source: Donor-specific differences in efficiency of HBV infection were observed consistent with variable HBV permissiveness of primary human hepatocytes (Shlomai et al., 2014), while HBV infection was observed with similar efficiency in different passages of the same donor line (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–D.

claim: Infection of hD organoids with organoid-produced HBV resulted in expression of intracellular HBV RNA.
source: As shown in Figure 1H, infection of hD organoids with organoid-produced HBV resulted in expression of intracellular HBV RNA, indicating that organoids produce infectious viral particles.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Organoids produce infectious viral particles.
source: As shown in Figure 1H, infection of hD organoids with organoid-produced HBV resulted in expression of intracellular HBV RNA, indicating that organoids produce infectious viral particles.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 1H demonstrating that organoid-produced virus can infect new organoids.

claim: Differentiated organoids were able to support infection and replication when challenged with HBV-infected patient sera.
source: However, differentiated organoids were able to support infection and replication when challenged with HBV-infected patient sera, as shown by production of viral DNA, expression of viral transcripts, and positive immunostaining for HBV surface antigen (HBsAg) (Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Tenofovir is a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor that inhibits the reverse transcription of HBV pre-genomic RNA to DNA.
source: Tenofovir is a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor that inhibits the reverse transcription of HBV pre-genomic RNA to DNA.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about the mechanism of action of tenofovir.

claim: Fialuridine is a nucleoside analog that inhibits reverse transcription and was shown to cause severe hepatotoxicity in patients.
source: Fialuridine, also a nucleoside analog that inhibits reverse transcription, was shown to cause severe hepatotoxicity in patients (McKenzie, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (McKenzie, 1995).

claim: HBV viral DNA production in the culture supernatant was inhibited by both tenofovir and fialuridine in three independent hD-derived organoids, whereas RNA levels remained the same.
source: In the organoids, HBV viral DNA production in the culture supernatant was inhibited by both tenofovir and fialuridine in three independent hD-derived organoids, whereas, as expected, RNA levels remained the same (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Treatment of HepG2.2.15 cells with tenofovir and fialuridine resulted in similar decreases in released HBV DNA, but no change in intracellular HBV RNA levels.
source: As expected, treatment of HepG2.2.15 cells with tenofovir and fialuridine resulted in similar decreases in released HBV DNA, but no change in intracellular HBV RNA levels (Figure 2C), reaffirming the mechanism of action of these drugs in a cell-line model of HBV replication.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: HepG2 cells demonstrated no change in cell viability upon treatment with tenofovir and increasing concentrations of fialuridine as compared to the mock-treated cells.
source: HepG2 cells demonstrated no change in cell viability upon treatment with tenofovir and increasing concentrations of fialuridine as compared to the mock-treated cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The phenotype of HepG2 cells was comparable across all treatments as observed by microscopy.
source: The phenotype of HepG2 cells was also comparable across all treatments as observed by microscopy (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Liver organoids treated with fialuridine at as low a concentration as 1 µM demonstrated a significant reduction in viability as measured by alamarBlue assay when compared to mock-treated cells.
source: Strikingly, the liver organoids treated with fialuridine at as low a concentration as 1 µM demonstrated a significant reduction in viability as measured by alamarBlue assay when compared to mock-treated cells (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Organoids treated with higher fialuridine concentrations (5–20 µM) as well as with 20 µM tenofovir demonstrated impaired viability.
source: The organoids treated with higher fialuridine concentrations (5–20 µM) as well as with 20 µM tenofovir also demonstrated impaired viability (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Fialuridine-induced toxicity is evident and quantifiable in the primary human liver organoid model but not in the HepG2.2.15 model of HBV replication.
source: This highlights that fialuridine-induced toxicity is evident and quantifiable in the primary human liver organoid model but not in the HepG2.2.15 model of HBV replication.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of experimental data from organoids and HepG2 cells.

claim: Higher HBV infection efficiency in DM organoids correlated with higher levels of NTCP expression.
source: We observed higher HBV infection efficiency in DM organoids as compared to EM organoids (Figure 1C). This correlated with higher levels of sodium taurocholate co-transporting polypeptide (NTCP) expression, a cellular receptor expressed on the surface of hepatocytes implicated in HBV entry (Yan et al., 2012), in differentiated organoids as compared to organoids in EM (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1C and 3A-B, and a citation to published literature (Yan et al., 2012).

claim: NTCP is a cellular receptor expressed on the surface of hepatocytes implicated in HBV entry.
source: This correlated with higher levels of sodium taurocholate co-transporting polypeptide (NTCP) expression, a cellular receptor expressed on the surface of hepatocytes implicated in HBV entry (Yan et al., 2012), in differentiated organoids as compared to organoids in EM (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Yan et al., 2012).

claim: HBV infection of liver organoids was dependent on NTCP as (pre)treatment with the competitive entry inhibitor myrcludex-B decreased infection of organoids.
source: HBV infection of liver organoids was dependent on NTCP as (pre)treatment with the competitive entry inhibitor myrcludex-B decreased infection of organoids as shown by quantitation of HBV intracellular RNA (Figure 3C) as well as HBV DNA (Figure 3D) and HBeAg (Figure 3E) in the supernatant of infected organoids.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3C, 3D, and 3E.

claim: Exogenous expression of NTCP in hepatoma cell lines was shown to confer susceptibility to infection.
source: Exogenous expression of NTCP in hepatoma cell lines was shown to confer susceptibility to infection (Yan et al., 2012) in line with our observations of increased HBV infection in differentiated organoids, likely because of the higher level of NTCP expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Yan et al., 2012).

claim: Comparable levels of HBV DNA and HBsAg were observed in the supernatants of both parental and NTCP-expressing organoid lines.
source: Interestingly, comparable levels of HBV DNA and HBsAg were observed in the supernatants of both parental and NTCP-expressing organoid lines (Figure 3I–J), suggesting that expression of NTCP alone is not sufficient to improve HBV infection rate in liver organoids grown in EM (Figure 3I–J and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3I-J and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Expression of NTCP alone is not sufficient to improve HBV infection rate in liver organoids grown in EM.
source: Interestingly, comparable levels of HBV DNA and HBsAg were observed in the supernatants of both parental and NTCP-expressing organoid lines (Figure 3I–J), suggesting that expression of NTCP alone is not sufficient to improve HBV infection rate in liver organoids grown in EM (Figure 3I–J and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data shown in Figures 3I-J and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Lenti-HBV allowed for the generation of replication-competent, expandable, long-term, hD transgenic lenti-HBV organoid lines, in which transcription from the HBV transgene results in the production of viral proteins and particles.
source: 'Lenti-HBV' (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–D) allowed for the generation of replication-competent, expandable, long-term, hD transgenic lenti-HBV organoid lines, in which transcription from the HBV transgene results in the production of viral proteins and particles (Figure 3K–L, Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3K-L and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C-D.

claim: Organoid cultures were generated from fresh and frozen explant tissue from all donors with similar efficiency.
source: We generated and expanded organoid cultures from fresh and frozen explant tissue from all donors with similar efficiency (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is stated but data is not shown in the manuscript.

claim: Non-tumor HBV-infected patient-derived (iP) organoids displayed proliferation rates comparable to those of hD organoids.
source: Non-tumor HBV-infected patient-derived (infected patient [iP]) organoids were expanded in culture (EM) and displayed proliferation rates (Figure 4B and data not shown) and expression of progenitor markers LGR5, KRT7, HNF4α, and Sox9 (Figure 4C) comparable to those of hD organoids.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: Non-tumor HBV-infected patient-derived organoids displayed expression of progenitor markers LGR5, KRT7, HNF4α, and Sox9 comparable to those of hD organoids.
source: Non-tumor HBV-infected patient-derived (infected patient [iP]) organoids were expanded in culture (EM) and displayed proliferation rates (Figure 4B and data not shown) and expression of progenitor markers LGR5, KRT7, HNF4α, and Sox9 (Figure 4C) comparable to those of hD organoids.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In DM, both hD and iP liver organoid cultures showed increased expression of hepatocyte-specific genes encoding albumin, cytochrome CYP3A4, and NTCP, concomitant with decreased expression of the stem cell-specific gene LGR5.
source: In DM, both hD and iP liver organoid cultures showed increased expression of hepatocyte-specific genes encoding albumin, cytochrome CYP3A4, and NTCP, the cellular receptor implicated in HBV hepatocyte entry, concomitant with decreased expression of the stem cell-specific gene LGR5 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: None of the iP organoids showed signs of HBV production at the RNA, DNA, or protein level.
source: None of the iP organoids showed signs of HBV production at the RNA, DNA, or protein level (data not shown), suggesting that adult stem cells, from which the liver organoids are derived, do not contain actively replicating HBV.
evidence: This claim is stated but data is not shown in the manuscript.

claim: Adult stem cells, from which the liver organoids are derived, do not contain actively replicating HBV.
source: None of the iP organoids showed signs of HBV production at the RNA, DNA, or protein level (data not shown), suggesting that adult stem cells, from which the liver organoids are derived, do not contain actively replicating HBV.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that iP organoids showed no signs of HBV production.

claim: Five out of six iP organoids contained portions of integrated HBV, corresponding to the HBx coding region.
source: Interestingly, five out of six iP organoids contained portions of integrated HBV, corresponding to the HBx coding region (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In previous genome-wide analyses in tissues derived from donors with HCC, the HBx region of the HBV genome was found to be highly integrated in both HCC and non-tumor hepatocytes from infected patients.
source: In accordance with our findings, in previous genome-wide analyses in tissues derived from donors with HCC, this region of the HBV genome was also found to be highly integrated in both HCC and non-tumor hepatocytes from infected patients (Sung et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Sung et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2016).

claim: In one donor who was previously infected with HBV but cleared the infection (iDonor1), integration corresponding to a part of the HBV genome, including the HBx region, was observed.
source: Interestingly, in one donor, who was previously infected with HBV but cleared the infection (iDonor1), integration corresponding to a part of the HBV genome, including the HBx region, was also observed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Despite clearance of active HBV replication, portions of the genome may remain integrated in the hepatocyte genome.
source: This finding indicates that despite clearance of active HBV replication, portions of the genome may remain integrated in the hepatocyte genome, for which the functional consequences remain to be elucidated.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of HBV integration in iDonor1.

claim: Differentiated iP organoids showed hepatocyte morphology and physiology comparable to hD organoids.
source: At the phenotypic level, while EM organoids grew larger in size and were translucent, differentiated iP organoids showed hepatocyte morphology and physiology comparable to hD organoids, with thickening of the outer cell layer, comparable to hD organoids (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A) and production of albumin as detected by immunofluorescence staining (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: The iP organoid lines were seeded from five HBV mono-infected patients with cirrhotic liver, four of whom presented with small tumors at the time of the explant.
source: The iP organoid lines were seeded from five HBV mono-infected patients with cirrhotic liver, four of whom presented with small tumors at the time of the explant (Figure 5A, Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by information in Figure 5A and Table 1.

claim: Although the hD and iP organoids were phenotypically indistinguishable, the iP organoids clustered separately from the healthy donors.
source: Interestingly, although the hD and iP organoids were phenotypically indistinguishable, the iP organoids clustered separately from the healthy donors (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A gene signature characteristic of iP-derived organoids was identified.
source: This comparison resulted in identification of a gene signature characteristic of iP-derived organoids (henceforth 'iP-signature') (Figure 5A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: A group of 33 putative early biomarker genes was identified.
source: We then ranked the differentially expressed genes according to the relative distance of their expression in hD- vs iP-derived organoids and identified a group of 33 putative early biomarker genes (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The 'early signature' genes were enriched in metabolic pathway-associated genes.
source: Gene ontology (GO)-term and KEGG-pathway analysis revealed that the 'early signature' genes were enriched in metabolic pathway-associated genes (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis results shown in Supplementary file 2.

claim: CCNA1 and STMN2, which were found to be upregulated in the non-tumor infected patient-derived organoids, were previously identified to be upregulated in HCC.
source: Among these, CCNA1 and STMN2, which we found to be upregulated in the non-tumor infected patient-derived organoids, were previously identified to be upregulated in HCC (Allain et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2008; Paradis et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the current study and citations to published literature (Allain et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2008; Paradis et al., 2003).

claim: WNK2, RUSC2, CYP3A4, and RGN, among the significantly downregulated genes in the non-tumor iP organoids, have been described as tumor suppressors downregulated in HCC.
source: Conversely, WNK2, RUSC2, CYP3A4, and RGN, among the significantly downregulated genes in the non-tumor iP organoids, have been described as tumor suppressors downregulated in HCC (Allain et al., 2016; Ashida et al., 2017; Tao et al., 2011; Yamaguchi, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the current study and citations to published literature (Allain et al., 2016; Ashida et al., 2017; Tao et al., 2011; Yamaguchi, 2015).

claim: Upregulation of mRNA expression of the organoid-derived signature genes ADAMTS1, CORO1A, PTHLH, STMN2, and STY5 was observed in primary hepatocytes obtained from HBV-infected patients as compared to those obtained from healthy donors.
source: Indeed, we observed upregulation of mRNA expression of the organoid-derived signature genes ADAMTS1, CORO1A, PTHLH, STMN2, and STY5 in primary hepatocytes obtained from HBV-infected patients as compared to those obtained from healthy donors (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Signature genes were upregulated upon ex vivo HBV infection of hD organoids.
source: Similarly, signature genes were upregulated upon ex vivo HBV infection of hD organoids (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The organoids generated from the iDonors, which had cleared HBV infection, clustered together and more closely to the larger group of iP organoids derived from patients with HBV-driven cirrhosis and HCC.
source: Interestingly, the organoids generated from the iDonors (light orange bars), which had cleared HBV infection, clustered together and more closely to the larger group of iP organoids derived from patients with HBV-driven cirrhosis and HCC (maroon bars) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The observation of iDonors' clustering closely with iP-HBV-HCC indicated the presence of the early HCC-like gene signature in these infected donor livers, despite clearance of HBV infection and absence of phenotypic and functional abnormalities at the time of donation.
source: This observation of iDonors' clustering closely with iP-HBV-HCC indicated the presence of the early HCC-like gene signature in these infected donor livers, despite clearance of HBV infection and absence of phenotypic and functional abnormalities at the time of donation, an observation that may be important to be considered for transplantation purposes and surveillance.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the clustering analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The iP-signature separates and groups together the non-infected samples and iP organoids.
source: The iP-signature separates and groups together the non-infected samples (gray bars) and iP organoids (black bars) (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Although the CN samples were obtained from cirrhotic livers, they grouped apart from the HBV-infected iPs and hDs.
source: Importantly, although the CN samples were obtained from cirrhotic livers (green bars), they grouped apart from the HBV-infected iPs and hDs (Figure 6C–D), indicating that our gene signature is defined by HBV-infection status, rather than the cirrhotic status.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6C-D.

claim: The gene signature is defined by HBV-infection status, rather than the cirrhotic status.
source: Importantly, although the CN samples were obtained from cirrhotic livers (green bars), they grouped apart from the HBV-infected iPs and hDs (Figure 6C–D), indicating that our gene signature is defined by HBV-infection status, rather than the cirrhotic status.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the clustering analysis shown in Figures 6C-D.

claim: All hD organoids are clearly separated from the rest and tightly grouped together, while the iP organoids form separate groups corresponding to HDV coinfection, HCC, acute liver failure, or previous/cirrhotic HBV infection and cluster together, but away from CN samples.
source: In agreement, multidimensional scaling analysis of all iP and hD samples indicated that all hD organoids are clearly separated from the rest and tightly grouped together, while the iP organoids form separate groups corresponding to HDV (hepatitis D virus) coinfection, HCC, acute liver failure, or previous/cirrhotic HBV infection and cluster together, but away from CN samples (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6A-D.

claim: The application of the gene signature when mapped onto the relevant TCGA gene expression data distinctly separated the TCGA HCC samples from non-HCC samples.
source: The application of this gene signature when mapped onto the relevant TCGA gene expression data distinctly separated the TCGA HCC samples from non-HCC samples (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Transcriptomic analysis of patient-derived liver organoid model identified a novel early liver cancer gene signature in non-tumor HBV-infected patient-derived liver organoids, despite the absence of phenotypic signs of aberrant growth.
source: This important observation indicates that transcriptomic analysis of our patient-derived liver organoid model identified a novel early liver cancer gene signature in non-tumor HBV-infected patient-derived liver organoids, despite the absence of phenotypic signs of aberrant growth.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined results of the transcriptomic analysis and clustering with TCGA data.

claim: Human liver organoids serve as a novel in vitro primary model system that supports HBV infection and replication.
source: Human liver organoids are a novel in vitro primary model system that supports HBV infection and replication, can be utilized as a platform to study HBV pathogenesis as well as for potential anti-HBV-drug screening, can be transgenically modified for downstream mechanistic and functional assays, and can be seeded from HBV-infected patient livers for personalized molecular and functional analyses (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Human liver organoids can be utilized as a platform to study HBV pathogenesis as well as for potential anti-HBV-drug screening.
source: Human liver organoids are a novel in vitro primary model system that supports HBV infection and replication, can be utilized as a platform to study HBV pathogenesis as well as for potential anti-HBV-drug screening, can be transgenically modified for downstream mechanistic and functional assays, and can be seeded from HBV-infected patient livers for personalized molecular and functional analyses (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Human liver organoids can be transgenically modified for downstream mechanistic and functional assays.
source: Human liver organoids are a novel in vitro primary model system that supports HBV infection and replication, can be utilized as a platform to study HBV pathogenesis as well as for potential anti-HBV-drug screening, can be transgenically modified for downstream mechanistic and functional assays, and can be seeded from HBV-infected patient livers for personalized molecular and functional analyses (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Human liver organoids can be seeded from HBV-infected patient livers for personalized molecular and functional analyses.
source: Human liver organoids are a novel in vitro primary model system that supports HBV infection and replication, can be utilized as a platform to study HBV pathogenesis as well as for potential anti-HBV-drug screening, can be transgenically modified for downstream mechanistic and functional assays, and can be seeded from HBV-infected patient livers for personalized molecular and functional analyses (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Healthy donor liver organoids were efficiently infected with both recombinant virus as well as HBV-infected patient serum.
source: Healthy donor liver organoids were efficiently infected with both recombinant virus as well as HBV-infected patient serum, expressed HBsAg, HBeAg, and HBV core proteins, produced cccDNA and infectious HBV in the culture supernatant, indicating that liver organoids support the full HBV replication cycle (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Infected healthy donor liver organoids expressed HBsAg, HBeAg, and HBV core proteins.
source: Healthy donor liver organoids were efficiently infected with both recombinant virus as well as HBV-infected patient serum, expressed HBsAg, HBeAg, and HBV core proteins, produced cccDNA and infectious HBV in the culture supernatant, indicating that liver organoids support the full HBV replication cycle (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Infected healthy donor liver organoids produced cccDNA and infectious HBV in the culture supernatant.
source: Healthy donor liver organoids were efficiently infected with both recombinant virus as well as HBV-infected patient serum, expressed HBsAg, HBeAg, and HBV core proteins, produced cccDNA and infectious HBV in the culture supernatant, indicating that liver organoids support the full HBV replication cycle (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Liver organoids support the full HBV replication cycle.
source: Healthy donor liver organoids were efficiently infected with both recombinant virus as well as HBV-infected patient serum, expressed HBsAg, HBeAg, and HBV core proteins, produced cccDNA and infectious HBV in the culture supernatant, indicating that liver organoids support the full HBV replication cycle (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental observations shown in Figure 1.

claim: The ex vivo infected organoid replication platform is amenable to screening for potential inhibitors of HBV replication and can provide insights into both HBV-directed anti-viral activity and drug-induced toxicity.
source: We demonstrated that the ex vivo infected organoid replication platform is amenable to screening for potential inhibitors of HBV replication and can provide insights into both HBV-directed anti-viral activity and drug-induced toxicity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data on drug screening presented in Figure 2.

claim: The ability to measure different readouts of HBV replication at the level of HBV mRNA gene expression, or viral production by quantitation of HBV DNA or S antigen, present in the culture supernatant of HBV-infected liver organoids, can provide insights into the distinct steps in the HBV life cycle that may be targeted upon drug treatment.
source: The ability to measure different readouts of HBV replication at the level of HBV mRNA gene expression, or viral production by quantitation of HBV DNA or S antigen, present in the culture supernatant of HBV-infected liver organoids, can provide insights into the distinct steps in the HBV life cycle that may be targeted upon drug treatment.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental approach and results shown in Figure 2.

claim: Fialuridine treatment of HBV-infected human liver organoids efficiently inhibited HBV replication but also caused significant toxicity in the liver organoids.
source: While fialuridine treatment of HBV-infected human liver organoids efficiently inhibited HBV replication, it also caused significant toxicity in the liver organoids.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: A phase II clinical trial conducted in 1993 to evaluate fialuridine as a novel HBV-anti-viral drug was terminated on an emergency basis by week 13 because of serious hepatotoxicity in seven patients, of which five died and two required emergency liver transplantation.
source: Although the preliminary results of the trial were promising, with reduced levels of HBV DNA in patients, the study was terminated on an emergency basis by week 13 because of serious hepatotoxicity in seven patients, of which five died and two required emergency liver transplantation (McKenzie, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (McKenzie, 1995).

claim: The expression of a nucleoside transporter in human mitochondria may be responsible for the human-specific mitochondrial toxicity caused by fialuridine.
source: This compound successfully passed pre-clinical toxicity studies, but the expression of a nucleoside transporter in human mitochondria may be responsible for the human-specific mitochondrial toxicity caused by fialuridine (Lee et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Lee et al., 2006).

claim: In the primary human liver organoid system, the toxicity of fialuridine is significant and quantifiable but was not observed in the human HepG2 hepatoma cell line.
source: In the primary human liver organoid system, the toxicity of fialuridine is significant and quantifiable (Figure 2E–F) but was not observed in the human HepG2 hepatoma cell line, indicating that human liver organoids can more accurately predict the clinical outcomes of drug treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2E-F.

claim: Human liver organoids can more accurately predict the clinical outcomes of drug treatment than HepG2 cells.
source: In the primary human liver organoid system, the toxicity of fialuridine is significant and quantifiable (Figure 2E–F) but was not observed in the human HepG2 hepatoma cell line, indicating that human liver organoids can more accurately predict the clinical outcomes of drug treatment.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of fialuridine toxicity in organoids versus HepG2 cells and the known clinical outcomes.

claim: HepG2 cell lines exogenously expressing NTCP, while susceptible to infection, are inefficiently infected with HBV and require high viral titers.
source: Consistent with our observations, HepG2 cell lines exogenously expressing NTCP, while susceptible to infection, are inefficiently infected with HBV and require high viral titers (Iwamoto et al., 2014; Yan et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Iwamoto et al., 2014; Yan et al., 2012).

claim: The observations are suggestive of the potential necessity for additional (co)receptors or downstream factors necessary for optimal infection in hepatocytes.
source: These observations are suggestive of the potential necessity for additional (co)receptors or downstream factors necessary for optimal infection in hepatocytes.
evidence: This claim is speculative and inferred from the observation that NTCP overexpression alone is not sufficient for optimal infection.

claim: The lentiviral HBV model, although not a cccDNA-generating model of productive HBV infection, is a useful primary human liver model to investigate HBV transcription and HBV-directed drugs.
source: This model, similar to HepG2.2.15 cells, although not a cccDNA-generating model of productive HBV infection, is a useful primary human liver model to investigate HBV transcription and HBV-directed drugs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the characteristics of the lentiviral HBV model described in the manuscript.

claim: The human liver organoid platform offers the advantage that HBV-infected patient-derived organoids resemble the diseased tissue of origin.
source: However, the human liver organoid platform offers two main advantages over these model systems. The first and most important is that HBV-infected patient-derived organoids resemble the diseased tissue of origin, as demonstrated by our gene expression studies (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The organoid platform allows the possibility of expansion and biobanking, ensuring the availability of sufficient samples for downstream analyses.
source: Second, the organoid platform allows the possibility of expansion and biobanking, ensuring the availability of sufficient samples for downstream analyses.
evidence: This claim is based on the established characteristics of organoid culture systems.

claim: The observed HBV-infected patient-specific gene expression profile is likely a marker of HBV infection and possibly HBx expression.
source: Thus, the observed HBV-infected patient-specific gene expression profile is likely a marker of HBV infection and possibly HBx expression.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of HBx integration and the gene expression patterns.

claim: The gene expression profile of the tumor microenvironment may serve as an important biomarker of HCC as bystander cells contain portions of the integrated HBV genome and are chronically exposed to released HBV proteins despite not having active viral replication.
source: Our observations are consistent with the notion that the gene expression profile of the tumor microenvironment may serve as an important biomarker of HCC as bystander cells contain portions of the integrated HBV genome and are chronically exposed to released HBV proteins despite not having active viral replication.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined observations of HBV integration, gene expression patterns, and lack of active viral replication.

claim: HBV-infected non-tumor patient-derived liver organoids exhibit an early cancer gene profile.
source: Indeed, our data indicate that HBV-infected non-tumor patient-derived liver organoids exhibit an early cancer gene profile, as shown by comparison to the TCGA-LIHC database.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing organoid gene expression to TCGA-LIHC database.

claim: The identification of early aberrant gene regulatory networks and biomarkers that drive HBV-mediated HCC, detectable at an early non-tumor stage without phenotypic signs of tumorigenesis, allows for patient-specific surveillance of disease progression.
source: The identification of early aberrant gene regulatory networks and biomarkers that drive HBV-mediated HCC, detectable at an early non-tumor stage without phenotypic signs of tumorigenesis, allows for patient-specific surveillance of disease progression and provides a screening platform for candidate drugs that may guide personalized treatments by targeting early stages in HBV-mediated HCC.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the identification of the early cancer gene signature in non-tumor organoids.

claim: The identification of early biomarkers provides a screening platform for candidate drugs that may guide personalized treatments by targeting early stages in HBV-mediated HCC.
source: The identification of early aberrant gene regulatory networks and biomarkers that drive HBV-mediated HCC, detectable at an early non-tumor stage without phenotypic signs of tumorigenesis, allows for patient-specific surveillance of disease progression and provides a screening platform for candidate drugs that may guide personalized treatments by targeting early stages in HBV-mediated HCC.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the identification of the early cancer gene signature and the potential applications of the organoid platform.
